To use あげる (I give to someone else) and くれる (someone else gives to me).
To use もらう (I receive from someone, with に or から).
To say what you do for others: ～て あげる.
To thank people for what they did for you: ～て くれました, ～て もらいました.

a-ge-ru, ku-re-ru, mo-ra-u: three short verbs; practise them in pairs with a gesture (towards someone else, towards you, receiving).

1. あげる and くれる
In Japanese the DIRECTION of a gift matters. If the gift goes from you to someone else: あげる. If it comes towards you (or your group: family, close friends): くれる.
You can’t say “ケンジさん が わたし に あげました”. When YOU receive something, the verb is always くれる.
もらう looks at it from the receiver’s side. The giver is marked with に or から:
I received a cloth from Mrs Suzuki.
Mrs Suzuki gave me a cloth. (the same fact)
The same fact can be said in two ways: X が くれました (focus on the giver) or X に もらいました (focus on you, the receiver).
3. Favours: ～て あげる / ～て くれる / ～て もらう
The same three verbs go after the ～て form to show that someone does an ACTION for someone else’s benefit:
I do something for someone else
someone else does something for me
～て あげる said directly to someone can sound arrogant (“I’m doing you a favour”). For polite offers, rather say ～ましょう か: もちましょう か (shall I carry it for you?).
The most natural thank-you formula: ～て くれて ありがとう / ～て くださって ありがとう ございます (polite).
I borrowed the dress from Carmen.
かす = to lend (like あげる), かりる = to borrow (like もらう). The logic is the same as with gifts.

ふみこさん の はじめて の りょこう — Mrs Fumiko’s first trip
Mrs Fumiko is seventy-two. But until now she had never left Japan.
It was her first time on a plane too. The fourteen-hour flight was very long.
A young woman in the next seat was very kind to her.
She showed her how to ask for a drink, looked at the clouds outside with her and so on.
At Madrid airport, Mihai and Ana were waiting for her.
They had written “Welcome, Mrs Fumiko” on a big sheet of paper and were holding it up.
Mihai had written the kanji part by himself. It was a bit crooked, but Mrs Fumiko could read it straight away.
“Mihai! Did you write these characters for me?”
“Yes. Because you taught me kanji. Through your letter.”
Mrs Fumiko laughed and shook Mihai’s hand.
Mrs Suzuki was waiting at the airport exit. Tama was minding the house.
The two sisters hugged for a while, without saying anything.
The two of them, who hadn’t spoken for so long, were now in the same country.
From the next day, Ana showed Mrs Fumiko around Madrid.
At the Prado museum, Mrs Fumiko stood motionless for a long time in front of the Goya paintings.
In Retiro Park they went out in a rowing boat. Mihai rowed for them.
At the churros café, Carmen showed them how to drink hot chocolate.
“You eat something this sweet in the morning?” Mrs Fumiko was amazed. But she had a second one.
On the evening of the third day, Mrs Fumiko opened her big bag.
“I have a present for each of you.”
She gave Carmen tea from Kyoto. She gave Elena a beautiful fan.
She gave Ana a little box. Inside was a hairpin with a white flower.
“This is the hairpin our mother wore at her wedding.”
Ana, astonished, looked at Mrs Suzuki. Mrs Suzuki gave a little nod.
“I talked it over with my sister. We both thought we wanted to give it to you.”
“Please accept it. If it weren’t for you two, we would never have been able to talk again.”
Finally, Mrs Fumiko gave Mihai a long scroll of paper.
When he unrolled it, a single large kanji was written in black ink.
“It’s your first kanji, isn’t it? My sister told me.”
“Hang it in your home. A mountain doesn’t move. May your marriage be as strong as a mountain.”
Mihai couldn’t say anything. He just bowed deeply.
That night, at home, Ana and Mihai thought about what to give in return.
“What could we give them? We’ve received so much.”
Ana answered, looking at the hairpin:
“Let me wear it at the wedding for them. Their mother’s hairpin. I think that’s the most beautiful thing we can give them in return.”
The next afternoon, Mrs Fumiko taught everyone origami.
Carmen made three cranes. Elena made a little boat.
Mihai’s crane wasn’t, however you looked at it, a crane.
“What’s this?” asked Mrs Fumiko, and Mihai answered with a straight face: “A mountain.”
Everyone laughed heartily. Mrs Suzuki and Mrs Fumiko laughed until they cried.
Just then Ana’s phone rang. It was a message from Haruka, in Hiroshima.
“Sakura and I arrive in Madrid next Monday. Please don’t tell Kenji.”
Ana smiled broadly and typed a reply: “We’ll come and pick you up at the airport!”
Mihai looked at the “mountain” on the table and thought: when Kenji finds out his family is coming, he’s sure to cry. And Sakura will take a photo of him right then.

interval (“nagai aida” = for a long time)
“yō ni naru” = to come to; “no yō ni” = like
“dō mite mo” = however you looked at it
